description:
This retrospective application seeks permission for the existing installation of a multi-split heat pump and air conditioning system serving six internal units at 29a Spencer Road. The installed system is sited to avoid material harm to the special architectural and historic character of the conservation area.
The external plant is modest in scale, with a combined volume of 0.32m3, representing 21% of the permitted development volume. It is positioned to the rear of the property and is not visible from public viewpoints or the highway, meaning it has no material impact on the appearance of the host building or the wider street scene. The proposal therefore respects the conservation area’s sensitivity to bulky additions, poor-quality alterations, and loss of architectural unity.
The installation does not alter the building pattern, roof form, front elevation, or principal public-facing character of the property. It also avoids the main pressures identified in the conservation area appraisal, namely loss of traditional character, loss of boundary treatments and garden space, loss of visual gaps, and the introduction of visually intrusive or poorly integrated plant and equipment. The rear-sited arrangement ensures that the proposal remains visually subordinate and consistent with the established form of development in this part of the conservation area.
The scheme also provides a clear environmental benefit by delivering a more efficient all-year heating and cooling solution than the existing central heating arrangement. This supports the sustainable upgrading of the building without compromising the qualities that make the conservation area special. In that regard, the proposal represents a balanced and low-impact retrofit that aligns with the council’s wider sustainability objectives.
The measured operational source noise level is 45dB, giving an estimated sound level of approximately 36dB at the property boundary with the most immediate neighbour, 29 Spencer Road, and approximately 30dB at the nearest neighbouring habitable-room receptor, being the first-floor bedroom window. This is below the 42dB threshold used in the MCS 020 planning noise standard for permitted-development assessment.
Overall, the proposal preserves the character and appearance of the area, avoids harm to residential amenity, and introduces a discreet low-carbon servicing solution that is appropriate to the site and its surroundings.
